**Answer: Yes.**

**Proof.**

The set $\mathbb{Q}$ is countably infinite. We construct a metric $d$ on $\mathbb{Q}$, defined without any reference to the usual real-valued structure of rationals, such that $(\mathbb{Q}, d)$ is compact.

**Construction.** Let
$$S = \{0\} \cup \left\{\tfrac{1}{n} : n \in \mathbb{N},\; n \geq 1\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}.$$
The set $S$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$, hence compact (Heine–Borel). It is countably infinite.

Since both $\mathbb{Q}$ and $S$ are countably infinite, there exists a bijection $\varphi : \mathbb{Q} \to S$. Define
$$d(p, q) := |\varphi(p) - \varphi(q)|, \qquad p, q \in \mathbb{Q}.$$

**$d$ is a metric.** Since $\varphi$ is injective, $d(p,q) = 0 \iff \varphi(p) = \varphi(q) \iff p = q$. Symmetry and the triangle inequality follow immediately from the corresponding properties of $|\cdot|$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

**$(\mathbb{Q}, d)$ is compact.** The map $\varphi : (\mathbb{Q}, d) \to (S, |\cdot|)$ is an isometry by construction: it is surjective and distance-preserving. Since $(S, |\cdot|)$ is compact and compactness is invariant under isometry, $(\mathbb{Q}, d)$ is compact.

**The metric is not the subspace metric from $\mathbb{R}$.** Under the standard metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(p,q) = |p - q|$ inherited from $\mathbb{R}$, the space $(\mathbb{Q}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is **not** compact (e.g., the open cover $\{(-n, n) \cap \mathbb{Q}\}_{n \geq 1}$ has no finite subcover, or equivalently $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ is not compact as it is not closed in $\mathbb{R}$). Since $(\mathbb{Q}, d)$ is compact while $(\mathbb{Q}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not, the two metrics are distinct — in fact not even topologically equivalent. The metric $d$ treats elements of $\mathbb{Q}$ merely as points of a countable set (relabeled by $\varphi$); the arithmetic/order structure of $\mathbb{Q}$ as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$ plays no role.

**Remark (generality).** The argument uses only countability. In fact, *every* countably infinite set admits a compact metric: biject it with $S$ above and pull back the metric. The specific identity of $\mathbb{Q}$ as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is irrelevant — only its cardinality $\aleph_0$ matters. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
